act1_quiz.prompt: It is mid-August in Eritrea's central highlands (Maekel). What seasonal and climate context should the duty analyst keep in mind when reading the rainfall forecast?
act1_quiz.hint: The highlands have one main wet season, and 2019's Indian Ocean state is unusual.
options: The kremti (kiremt) summer rains peak in July-August, and a developing positive Indian Ocean Dipole in 2019 is enhancing moisture supply to the Horn
August is the heart of the dry season, so any rain signal is almost certainly a model artefact
The highlands depend on the October-December short rains, which have not started yet
Rainfall here is controlled mainly by Atlantic hurricanes
act1_quiz.correct: The kremti (kiremt) summer rains peak in July-August, and a developing positive Indian Ocean Dipole in 2019 is enhancing moisture supply to the Horn
act1_quiz.answer_note: The Eritrean highlands receive most of their annual rainfall in the June-September kremti season, with peak intensity in July-August. In mid-2019 a strong positive Indian Ocean Dipole was developing, warming the western Indian Ocean and boosting moisture transport toward the Horn, so heavy-rain signals in this window deserve weight.
act1_quiz.bn_purpose: Driver and seasonal-calendar context that raises the prior on heavy-rain evidence during the August window.

act1_quiz.prompt: Why do Eritrea's central highlands pose a flash-flood rather than a slow riverine flood problem?
act1_quiz.hint: Picture rainfall landing on a steep plateau of 1,500-2,500 m drained by wadis.
options: Steep, short catchments drain the plateau through wadis, so intense convective rain converts to fast, high-energy runoff with very little lead time
Large permanent rivers take weeks to rise, giving long warning lead times
The terrain is flat and sandy, so water infiltrates before it can flow
Flooding only occurs from Red Sea storm surge reaching the highlands
act1_quiz.correct: Steep, short catchments drain the plateau through wadis, so intense convective rain converts to fast, high-energy runoff with very little lead time
act1_quiz.answer_note: The highland plateau sheds rain quickly into steep wadi systems draining toward the Mereb-Gash and Anseba basins. Flash floods here develop within hours of a convective storm, which is why the analyst must act on forecast tail signals rather than wait for observed river rises.
act1_quiz.bn_purpose: Why short-lead tail-risk evidence matters more than the ensemble mean in steep, fast-responding catchments.

decision.checkpoint_prompt: The ensemble mean may look benign but the tail signal is rising ahead of onset. What DOC level do you set, and why? A 'Watch + re-check + note the tail uncertainty' is a strong answer.

counterfactual.prompt: What if a precautionary no-regret action (alert highland communities and protect water crossings) were taken at the lead round on the tail signal?
counterfactual.narrative: Acting on a short-lead tail signal is exactly what the flood BN's tail_risk node exists to surface. The counterfactual illustrates loss reduction without claiming certainty.
